Use this sheet as an offline reference for the lecture and
[the code-reading activity](exercise-student.html). The comparison figures are
explained before the activity; they are not a second exercise. All summaries
use exact updating or supplied fits, with no new Stan inference.

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(posterior)
library(here)
source(here("R/functions.R"))
source(here("R/course_data.R"))
source(here("R/course_utils.R"))
source(here("R/course_visuals.R"))
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = FALSE,

  fig.width = 8,
  fig.height = 4.5
)

```

## Lecture reference: mother-tree comparison

```{r core-results}
fit <- course_fit("day3_trees")
trees <- make_tree_data()
knitr::kable(
  trees |> select(tree, n, suv) |> mutate(observed = suv / n),
  digits = 3
)
comparison <- mother_comparison(fit, seed = 42)
plot_mother_comparison(comparison)
plot_mother_truth(comparison, trees, highlight = "A", limits = c(.2, .5))
knitr::kable(
  comparison |> select(tree, n, model, mean, lower, upper),
  digits = 3
)
```

Purple open points show separate estimates; orange filled points show partial
pooling. The grey line and ribbon show the complete-pooling posterior mean and
95% credible interval; coloured bars are also 95% credible intervals. The line
is a comparison reference, not the exact target of hierarchical shrinkage.
Rows are ordered by separate posterior means, with seedling counts `n` shown;
the two sets of intervals are offset vertically within each tree.
The second plot uses the generating probabilities on x and posterior
means on y, with a dashed 1:1 reference. Arrows show movement
from Separate to Partial pooling. As in the lecture, Tree A is highlighted and
both axes run from 0.2 to 0.5. Tree G falls below this window; its estimates
remain in the full table. Truth is matched by tree ID.

The complete and separate models use flat Beta(1,1) priors on the probabilities.
The partial model uses a shared Normal distribution on the logit scale, with its
centre and SD estimated. Prior formulations also differ in this comparison.
Movement depends on group information and the inferred differences among trees.
It does not guarantee smaller error for every tree.

## Activity reference: Tree A's partial-pooling probability

Transform the saved logit-intercept draws before summarizing them. These are
probability draws, not future survivor counts.

```{r intercept-summary}
alpha_a <- fit$draws[["z[1]"]]
p_a <- plogis(alpha_a)
knitr::kable(
  tibble(
    tree = "A",
    mean = mean(p_a),
    lower = unname(quantile(p_a, 0.025)),
    upper = unname(quantile(p_a, 0.975))
  ),
  digits = 3
)
```

The mean and interval match Tree A's partial-pooling estimate in the lecture.
The activity asks readers to find the data, likelihood, shared prior and
probability transformation in the supplied code.

## Lecture reference: computational and predictive checks

```{r diagnostics}
knitr::kable(course_diagnostics(fit), digits = 2)
bayesplot::mcmc_trace(fit$draws, pars = c("mu", "sigma"))
plot_mother_check(fit)
```

Read sampler diagnostics and traces together. The predictive check generates
counts at the observed seedling numbers. Neither these checks nor the presence
of a grouping label alone establishes that sharing information is ecologically
appropriate.

## Lecture reference: return to regression

```{r regression-reference}
plot_cndd_species()
plot_cndd_abundance()
```

The lecture adds density, then allows intercepts and slopes to vary, then
introduces species abundance as a group-level predictor. These curves and
coefficients are conceptual simulations, not a fitted extension of the eight
mother trees or empirical results from the cited research.

The [expanded handout](exercise-student.html#from-intercepts-to-regression)
also contains an executed example with a new simulated CNDD data set, three
matching saved fits, fitted survival curves and an optional posterior predictive check.
It uses wood density as an alternative species-level predictor. Those fitted
results are separate from the conceptual lecture figures above.

## Optional reference: allometry and wood density

```{r allometry-reference}
plot_wood_density()
```

This plot uses a saved fit to simulated allometry data. The observation model
changes to Normal log height; information sharing among coefficients is the
common structure. It is outside the main activity.
